- **26.10.2026 (latest) - the Rollen screen stops promising what nothing enforces: 22 of its 32 checkboxes are now *disabled and visible* with a reason beside them (branch `work/roles-screen-honest`, PR against `staging`, browser only, no migration, no policy, no row written or deleted, nothing deployed).**
  - **The defect, re-verified read-only against production's catalogue rather than taken from the brief.** `src/components/RoleModal.tsx` draws 16 pages x 2 boxes, `Ansehen` and `Bearbeiten`, and **22 of the 32 store a value nothing ever reads**. So an administrator unticks *Ansehen* on Gehälter for `viewer`, gets a **success toast**, and that viewer goes on seeing Gehälter in the sidebar and reading every salary row.
  - **`can_view` is dead end to end, and the brief's count was low.** Every `current_role_permits` occurrence in a policy expression: **177, all `need_edit = true`, zero `false`** - the brief said 130, which has grown with later migrations. Every occurrence across function bodies in `public` and `app_private`: **23, all `true`, zero `false`**. The function has **no default** for that argument (`current_role_permits(p_page text, p_need_edit boolean)`), so nothing can reach the `ELSE rp.can_view` branch of its body. And there is **no `can(page, 'view')` call site in `src/`**: `AuthContext.can()` defaults its action to `'edit'`, the sidebar gates on `usePlan().can(item.feature)` - the **plan**, not the role - and the only occurrence in the tree is an assertion inside `companyScope.test.ts`.
  - **`Bearbeiten` is dead on six pages, for two different reasons, both measured.** `overview`, `statistics`, `accounting`: **zero mentions** in any policy expression or function body. `users`, `roles`, `settings`: their tables are gated by `is_company_admin()`, whose body (read from production) tests `user_profiles.role = 'admin'` and **never opens `role_permissions`**, and `CompanyAdminRoute` in `App.tsx` navigates a non-`admin` away from all three routes on the same test. The seeded `supervisor` holds `can_edit` on **all sixteen** - three rights nothing honours - and `editor` holds a dead one on `overview`.
  - **The owner refined option (a) and it is built that way: disabled, not removed.** His words were *"موافق — يبين انه موقوف ومعطل"* - agreed, but make it visible that it is stopped and disabled. So all 32 boxes are still drawn; 22 are `disabled`, show the **stored** value (not redrawn as unchecked) and are rendered at 50% opacity so "ticked but inert" cannot be read as "ticked and in force". Removal would have answered "where did the column go?" with silence.
  - **Three separate reasons, each as visible text under its section heading - never a tooltip.** A disabled input is skipped by the tab order, so a `title` or an `aria-describedby` alone is an explanation nobody is offered; `aria-describedby` is set as well because it costs nothing, and the test asserts the id it names is actually rendered. The sections are, live group first: **`Von der Rolle gesteuert`** (the ten, no excuse needed); **`Nur Unternehmens-Administratoren`** for `users`/`roles`/`settings`, which says the deciding fact is whether an account holds the role `admin` - a rule the user can act on, deliberately not the same sentence as the other group; and **`Nicht von der Rolle gesteuert`** for `overview`/`statistics`/`accounting`. The `Ansehen` column gets one sentence for the whole column under the table header, and the header itself reads the column name struck through with *stillgelegt* beneath it.
  - **THE PAYLOAD ANSWER, and it is the part most likely to be undone: `permissionPayload` is unchanged, byte for byte, and that is deliberate.** The form's state lives in `permissionMap`, not in the DOM, so a `disabled` box still carries its stored value into the payload. Stripping `can_view` "because it is dead" breaks it **twice**: a role with any edit right is refused outright as `edit_without_view` - and `company_role_save` compares with `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` exactly so that an **omitted** key refuses like a `false` one, because `=` made that guard fail **open** - while a view-only role is worse, because every entry drops out of `permissionPayload`'s filter, the payload becomes `[]`, and the RPC deletes all sixteen rows and inserts none: a role emptied with a success toast. **Measured on production: 20 stored rows are `can_view` true with `can_edit` false, sixteen of them `viewer`'s.** A test pins both halves and a mutation control shows the `[]` case printing `expected [] to have a length of 16`.
  - **The *edit implies view* guard is untouched.** `toggleEdit` still sets `can_view`, so the disabled `Ansehen` box **visibly moves** when the `Bearbeiten` box beside it is ticked. That is the database's rule made legible, not a glitch, and it is asserted rather than left to be noticed.

It is `grantedAreaCount` now - `can_edit` on the ten gated pages and nothing else - so that role reads *Keine wirksame Berechtigung* and `supervisor`'s sixteen edit rows read as ten.

- **25.10.2026 - routing moves onto the OSRM ridy already runs, through a gateway of our own that carries the limit (branch `work/osrm-shared-gateway`, PR against `staging`, no migration, no SQL, RLS kit not applicable, nothing deployed).** The owner decided that day not to build a routing dataset of ours: use theirs and connect to it, *without stopping it, bringing it down or putting pressure on their server*.
  - **THE STEP ONLY A PERSON CAN DO, and nothing works without it: `/usr/local/sbin/el-professor-release` must be reinstalled from `deploy/ci-release.sh` before the release that switches the profile.** That wrapper ships a fixed list of files and is installed on the host by hand. Until it is reinstalled, `deploy/osrm-gateway.conf` never leaves the archive - it is not stored with the release and not installed into the live checkout - and `deploy.sh` then refuses any release whose `COMPOSE_PROFILES` names `osrm-shared`, with exactly that sentence. A release that does **not** name the profile goes through unharmed, so merging this is safe on its own.
  - **The measurement, re-verified on 25.10.2026 and not taken from the brief.** One request each, Solingen -> Duesseldorf (`7.0845,51.1652;6.7735,51.2277`): ridy's `ridy-osrm-1` answered **30066.4 m / 2050.9 s** (`osrm/osrm-backend:latest`, `osrm-routed --algorithm mld /data/germany-latest.osrm`, read from `docker inspect`), ours **30131 m / 2025.3 s** (`nordrhein-westfalen-261020`, read from its own `ready.json`). **0.215 % apart on the distance** and 1.25 % on the duration - the brief's "0.2 %" is right about the distance only. Theirs covers all of Germany where ours can only ever cover one Land, so building ours is the worse answer as well as the dearer one.
  - **The design, and why the alias works.** `osrm-gateway` (nginx, the image `web` already pulls) sits on this stack's network under the **alias `osrm`** and on `ridy_default`, so `OSRM_ORIGIN` - `http://osrm:5000`, a constant in `_shared/travel-route-core.ts` - is unchanged and the edge function knows nothing about any of it. The decision lives in `COMPOSE_PROFILES`, where `deploy.sh` can refuse a bad one, which is the point of not making the address configuration.
  - **The sharpest trap, and it would have been silent: the gateway must NOT dial the name `osrm`.** On `ridy_default` that name is an alias of `ridy-osrm-1`; on ours it is now an alias of the gateway itself. A lookup of `osrm` from inside the gateway therefore matches on **both** of its networks, and nothing in Docker's resolver promises which answer comes back - some share of the requests would be the gateway proxying to itself. It dials `ridy-osrm-1`, which exists on one network only (verified: `ridy_default` aliases are `[ridy-osrm-1 osrm]`). **No claim is made here about the resolver's order**, because that is exactly the kind of thing this repository has read confidently and wrong; the design avoids needing to know.
  - **The same reasoning makes the two profiles mutually exclusive, and `deploy.sh` refuses both doors.** Our own `osrm` service answers to the name as its *service name*; the gateway answers to it by *alias*. With both profiles on, one name means two containers and `travel-route` reaches our own map or ridy's at random, per request, with nothing saying which answered. `compose_profiles_problem()` refuses the list, **first in its chain** so it cannot be masked by another complaint. And because a profile list cannot see a container that is already running - the switch-over release is exactly the one where ours is still up - `osrm_shared_conflict()` refuses before anything changes and prints the `docker rm -f` to type. `up -d --remove-orphans` is expected to take it away, but "expected" is not a guard.
  - **The volume guard stays with the old mode, and both halves are pinned.** `osrm_data_problem()` is asked only when the *rendered* config holds an `osrm` service, which the `osrm-shared` profile does not render, so it never fires in shared mode (there is no volume and no build); it still refuses a missing build in the old mode. A guard that fired in shared mode would refuse every release.
  - **The limits, and what each is based on.** 12 in flight is the product's own widest fan-out: the browser runs **3** calls at a time (`DEFAULT_CALL_CONCURRENCY`, `prefetch.ts`) and each call asks for **4** pairs at once (`CONCURRENCY`, `travel-route/index.ts`, **lowered from 8**), and 3 x 4 is that 12 - so one screen fits the budget exactly and never asks for more than it may have, while a second is slowed rather than doubling what reaches them. The three numbers are read from their own sources and multiplied out in a test, so none can be raised alone. 40 a second is what lets a month of rides finish: the rate and not the fan-out bounds such a run (a thousand pairs in 25 s, against over three minutes at the geocoder's 5), and the worst queue wait is 40/40 = **1 s**, inside the 3 s the function waits. Lowering the fan-out costs no throughput in shared mode for exactly that reason; against a container of our own it is the one thing it costs, and the stricter mode has to bind.
  - **WHAT 40 A SECOND COSTS THEIR SERVER IS NOT MEASURED, and the first version of this entry claimed it was.** It read "a few milliseconds of CPU for a 30 km MLD route, a fraction of one core" as if it had been timed. Only **one** request was ever made to their service, to compare its answer with ours, and that was not timed either. An MLD route query is cheap by OSRM's own design, but that is *read* and not measured - the exact kind of claim this repository has been wrong about. The rate is the one lever to lower if their owner reports load; it costs only wall-clock time on a screen somebody is watching, and lowering it is an edit to that line plus a redeploy, since the hash label recreates the container.
  - **Three defects were found in this branch's own work, recorded rather than quietly fixed.** (1) The job asked `edge-e2e` for `osrm-down` in **two** places, but a 502 from a gateway that is up is `service_error` and only an unresolvable name is `unreachable`, so the first call would have failed on the reason list; a new `upstream-down` mode asserts `service_error` and the test pins both. (2) **The alias check matched the service's own name, so it proved nothing** - `docker inspect` lists `osrm-gateway` in that alias list too, and a substring match for `osrm` would have passed with no alias at all, the alias being the whole design; the regex wants a whole word now and the step carries its own negative control. (3) The unmeasured-cost claim above. And a method note: the mutation harness was first piped through `head`, which killed it on **SIGPIPE before its restore step** and left a mutation in the working tree - caught by diffing against the backup, not by the tests.
  - **One path and one path only.** `GET /route/v1/driving/<lon,lat>;<lon,lat>`, two coordinates, matched by the location's own regex and rebuilt from a **named** capture. `/table` - an N x N matrix, by far the dearest thing OSRM offers - `/trip`, `/match`, `/nearest`, `/tile`, a third coordinate, another profile and another version are all 404 here and never reach them. The query is rebuilt (`overview=false&alternatives=false&steps=false&annotations=false`), so nobody who can reach the port can ask for a geometry, turn instructions or three routes.
  - **Two details that are easy to undo.** The capture is **named** because the method `if` evaluates `^(GET|HEAD)$`, which matches for a GET and replaces `$1` - a `$1` in the `proxy_pass` would have put the word "GET" into the path. And a refusal is a **503, never a 429**: `interpretOsrmAnswer` reads a 5xx with no OSRM `code` as `service_error`, where a 429 arrives as `bad_answer` and sends the next reader looking for a contract bug in OSRM's response instead of at this budget. 503 is also nginx's own default for both limits.
  - **What is given up, and nothing replaces it.** ridy's `osrm-routed` was started **without `--data_version`**, so no answer of theirs carries one, where our own build passes `--data_version osmosis`. `travel-route` reports `null` and `osrmSourceLabel()` prints `osrm` where it printed `osrm@2026-10`. **The month of the map is not knowable through this gateway.** Nothing breaks (the field is `string | null` the whole way through and the label already has that branch), but a figure loses its provenance.
  - **The stand-in can refuse, which is the lesson from the geocoder's 406.** `tests/deploy/osrm-gateway-stub.mjs` answers the real shape measured that day and models every refusal `osrm-routed` makes that we have to survive - `NoSegment`, `NoRoute`, `InvalidQuery`, `TooBig`, `InvalidService`, hanging, being slow, being absent - and **carries no `data_version`**, as theirs does not, so the cost above cannot be hidden by the test. Those 400 bodies carry the OSRM `code` the function reads, and the e2e proves nginx passes them through untouched: with `proxy_intercept_errors` every one of them would read `bad_answer`.
  - **The in-flight check needed the stand-in to be slow or it would have passed vacuously.** While they answer in milliseconds the rate alone keeps about one request in flight, so `mostInFlight <= 12` says nothing. A `slow` mode (500 ms, inside the 3 s read timeout) makes a flood pile up - 40 a second times 0.5 s is 20 - so the ceiling is actually reached and the assertion measures something.

The checks stand between a planning run and the **statutory documents that go to the Steuerberater**: a trip with no driver, a fourth Schicht in one day, a vehicle switch too short to be real. An override does not remove the failure, it **moves** it - from "the document cannot be downloaded" to "the wrong document was filed" - and the second is the expensive one, because nothing downstream re-checks what finalisation already passed. Where an operator is genuinely blocked the remedy is to correct the data the check is pointing at; a check that can be waived stops being a gate and becomes a warning, which is what the ten already are not. **Reverse it by asking** - the cost of the current behaviour is an operator who cannot finalise a month until the data is right, and that is a real cost, not a hypothetical one.

- **24.10.2026 - Phase 1 reports a same-vehicle overlapping block pair instead of emitting it silently (branch `feat/phase1-overlap-warning`, PR against `staging`, no migration, no SQL, nothing deployed).** This is the gap the entry below named and left open. `buildPhase1VehicleBlocks` emitted six coverage warning types - `duplicate_trip`, `missing_trip`, `canceled_in_block`, `block_too_long`, `block_gap_too_large`, `unsorted_blocks` (the union is one line in the file) - and **no overlap test of any kind**. It now emits a seventh, `block_overlap`, for two blocks of one vehicle whose time ranges intersect.
  - **Why Phase 1 can emit such a pair at all.** The max-duration split opens the next block at the next ride's **start**, and the walk is sorted by start only, so a **nested ride** - one that begins and ends inside a longer ride of the same vehicle - flushes the long ride as one block and opens a second block *inside* the first. A ride at 10:00-16:00 with one at 10:30-11:00 inside it, under a 4 h ceiling, gives blocks 10:00-16:00 and 10:30-11:00. Nothing downstream looks: Phase 3 cannot produce a driver overlap (`checkOverlap` at nine sites, `validateClone`, `purgeFinalConflicts`) and the finalization checks a driver and a vehicle switch, but **no code anywhere compares two blocks of one vehicle**.

Planning is daily and per vehicle, and a vehicle's own day is corrected at the source, not by the planner. Three tests assert the blocks, the trip coverage and the split counts are what they were.

Wiring the list itself through `engineText` would change what English users see for four messages that are not this task's, so it is named here rather than done.

A bare `HH:MM` comparison is the defect this shape avoids, and the cross-midnight and 25-hour-day (25.10.2026) tests are exactly its blind spots. - **24.10.2026 - a detected conflict, and the record of who reviewed it (branch `feat/conflict-review-record`, PR against `staging`, migration `20261023200000`, RLS kit run on the VPS: 131 migrations, 61 files, exit 0).** The product detects a great deal and stores almost none of it. `fahrtenbuch_trips.needs_review`, `planning_finalizations.is_stale`, the ten pre-finalisation checks, `warningCategories.classify()` and `tripAnalysis`'s twenty issue kinds had, between them, no reviewer, no decision and in most cases no storage at all - a finding was a string recomputed on every render. `partner_receipt_submissions` / `partner_note_submissions` are the one complete shape in the codebase (a `status` CHECK, `reviewed_by`, `reviewed_at`, a reason mandatory on the closing decision, a pointer to what the row became, no DELETE policy, an idempotency index and a queue index), and `public.conflict_reviews` is that shape applied to the detectors.
  - **What it can hold, and it is two detectors rather than five.** `trip_analysis` (the twenty `IssueType`s of `src/utils/tripAnalysis/`) and `return_check` (the six `AnomalyType`s of `src/utils/returnCheck/`). The test is not importance but whether the detector's output already carries a **stable identifier**, because an identifier that moves between releases cannot be the key of a stored decision. `tripAnalysis` builds `Issue.id` and is careful about what goes in it; `RideAnomaly` has no `id` but carries `(type, rideId)`, which is the same identity in two fields, composed into the same `kind:evidence` shape in one tested place.
  - **What it deliberately cannot hold, with the reason for each.** The **ten pre-finalisation checks** of `FinalizePlanningModal.tsx`: those are a gate - "there is no override", and documents are downloadable only once every one passes - so a reviewable record of a blocking check is a way past it, which is a product decision and not a storage question. **`warningCategories.classify()`**: it sorts warnings by matching German fragments, so its identifier is a sentence that any wording change renames, and a decision keyed on that is lost the first time somebody improves a message. **`fahrtenbuch_trips.needs_review` / `review_reasons`**: already stored and immutable after insert - an import-time fact about a row, not a finding to come back to; the engine's own row-quality kinds (`missing_start`, `end_before_start`, `ambiguous_local_time`) cover the same ground and do have a reviewable identity, so those are what land here. **`planning_finalizations.is_stale`**: already stored, and its only outcome is re-finalisation, so there is nothing to decide. **`OrderCheck` / `OrderPlacement`** from the Rückkehrpflicht tab: one row per completed ride is a record of every ride rather than of a conflict, and the two placements that read as reviewable (`away_from_base`, `block_start_away`) are exactly the ones the module says the file cannot decide - storing a decision against them is the one thing the "never a verdict" rule forbids. The six *anomalies* beside them are findings and are held.
  - **The idempotency key is `(company_id, detector, period_year, period_month, finding_key)`, and a re-run writes no second row** because `finding_key` names the **subject** of a finding and never its measurement or its evidence set. `driver_name_mismatch` is the engine's own proof: its id is `driver_name_mismatch:<driverId>` and not the list of misspelled rows, so a new row joining the evidence updates that finding instead of filing a second one. **Three things are deliberately not in the key.** The **algorithm version**: a decision is about a fact in the data, not about the code that noticed it, and putting the version in the key would discard every decision on the release that bumped it - which is the release where the review history is worth most. It is recorded instead, twice (`first_detected_version`, `last_detected_version`), so a reader can see the engine moved under a decision. The **measured values**: an overlap of 41 minutes re-measured at 42 is one conflict about one pair of rides. The **evidence set**, for the reason above. **One thing is in the key that no detector supplies: the period.** The engines analyse "the trips of a period" and carry no period field, so `no_shift_records:<driverId>` is the same string in September and October while being two different facts. `period_year` / `period_month` are **1-indexed**, as `fahrtenbuch_imports.month` is and *not* as `weekCalculations.ts` is. The cost is stated rather than hidden: a finding whose evidence straddles a month boundary is reported in both months and carries a decision in each, where the alternative silently applies September's decision to October's facts.
  - **A finding is a list to review, never a verdict**, and three parts of the schema are what keep it. `detector_status` carries the engines' three-valued honesty and **refuses `'passed'`**, so a clean check cannot be filed as a finding and the table cannot become a log of everything. The reviewer's words are **`acknowledged` and `dismissed`**, not `confirmed` and `rejected`: a detector's finding is not a fact a review can confirm; what a review can do is take it on or look and find nothing to act on. And the German is **the engine's own, carried with its dictionary key** (`explanation` + `explanation_key`), so a screen renders `engineText(...)` exactly as the panel does and the storage layer invents no vocabulary. Section 9 of the kit file reads the catalogue for all three and for a word-list (`verstoss`, `violation`, `schuld`, `strafe`, …) across every column name, constraint name and line of the guard. `ReturnCheckPanel.render.test.ts`, which fails the build on "Verstoß", is **untouched and passing**.

The asymmetry is deliberate: an acknowledged finding stays visible and remains actionable without justification, while a dismissed one with no reason cannot be told apart from one nobody examined. **There is no DELETE policy and no DELETE grant either**, so a client DELETE is `permission denied` rather than a statement that removes nothing while PostgREST answers 200 - the silent shape the partner tables still have. A company's rows go with the company, through the cascade.
  - **The guard derives what a client must not name.** `app_private.conflict_review_guard` stamps `reviewed_by` (`auth.uid()`), `reviewed_at` (`now()`) and `decided_values` - a copy of the measurement **as it stood when the decision was taken**, which is what tells a later reader whether the figures moved under it. It pins the finding's identity (detector, kind, key, year, month) so a dismissal of a trivial finding cannot be re-pointed at a serious one, pins `first_detected_at` / `first_detected_version` so an upsert cannot move them, and refuses a decision that **returns to `'open'`** - which is also what makes the client's upsert safe, because a re-run that carelessly sent `status: 'open'` fails loudly instead of quietly erasing every decision in the month. `reviewed_by` may be NULL on a decided row and `reviewed_at` may not, so the biconditional constraint is on the timestamp: a path with no session records a decision with no actor, as every NULL actor on `platform_staff` was written, and the screen says "Nicht erfasst" rather than this refusing a legitimate repair. **`company_id` is deliberately not pinned** - the four tenant policies already refuse a move, and a pin would make `matrix.sql`'s M probe answer T for the owner too, which is the one probe in that file that reaches a WITH CHECK clause at all.
  - **The defect I found in the branch I inherited, stated plainly: probe 6f measured the SELECT policy and not the WITH CHECK it names.** The first VPS run failed on `10m`, 6f's own mutation control - with the second copy of the UPDATE predicate dropped the move was expected to land, and it was still refused. Measured on PostgreSQL 17.6 with a throwaway diagnostic rather than reasoned about, five variants: plain `WHERE id` with the WITH CHECK as shipped → refused; plain `WHERE id` **with the WITH CHECK replaced by `true`** → **still refused**; cursor + `WHERE CURRENT OF` as shipped → refused; cursor **with the WITH CHECK `true`** → **the move lands**; SELECT policy `USING (true)` with the WITH CHECK as shipped → refused. An UPDATE whose `WHERE` reads a column has its **new** row checked against the SELECT policies as well, so a tenant-scoped SELECT policy refuses the move wherever the WITH CHECK would have allowed it - and **both raise the same `42501 new row violates row-level security policy`**. That is precisely the trap `matrix.sql` documents in its own header and takes its cursor for; this file had written the plain form, so it was a probe whose two refusals share a class, green with the clause it names removed entirely. 6f and 6g now move the row through `_cr_move_try` (a cursor and `WHERE CURRENT OF`), 10m goes through `_cr_move_mutant` and lands, and **10n is new**: the same mutation with a plain `WHERE` is still refused, recorded as a measurement so a later reader who finds the cursor fussy has to delete that line and say why. `_cr_move_try`'s header carries the five-row table.
  - **The second defect in the inherited work, smaller but able to break every insert: the module header claimed to omit a `NOT NULL` column.** `src/utils/conflictReviewRecord.ts` said `detectionPayload` carries neither `first_detected_at` nor `first_detected_version`. It carries the second, and it has to - `conflict_reviews.first_detected_version` is `NOT NULL` with no default, so an insert omitting it fails `23502` and every first sighting of every finding is lost. The guard pins it back on the UPDATE half of the same upsert, which is what makes sending it harmless and which kit probe 4c already measures (a re-run under `cr/2.0.0` leaves the row at `cr/1.0.0`) - but it can only pin it to an older row, and a first sighting has none. The existing test asserted only that `first_detected_at` is absent, so a reader following the header would have deleted the key and learned it from a failed batch. The asymmetry is pinned from both sides now, and the new control was watched failing: with the key removed from `DETECTION_PAYLOAD_KEYS` it prints `expected [ 'company_id', 'detector', …(17) ] to include 'first_detected_version'`. Header and test only; no column, constraint, policy, trigger or payload value changed, and `git diff` over `supabase/migrations/**`, `tests/**` and the kit runner is empty against the tree the kit ran on.
  - **Section 11 also asserts the probe COUNT before the verdict**, which it did not. "No row failed" is not the claim "every probe ran": a section that returns early leaves a shorter table and a passing verdict, and a sibling kit file reported "all 34 probes matched" with three rows missing - the three being exactly its mutation controls. The number is 102 and is not a floor, because a number that only ever grew would not catch a probe replaced by a weaker one.

All fourteen moved, and the baseline is clean on either side.
  - **The two context triggers are both on the table**, keyed on the policies naming `get_active_company_id()` and not on who writes it today - `20260924100000` shipped with neither on the reasoning "no client writes it" and the kit refused it. Section 8 measures them live: a `view` context reads the company it opened and writes nothing (`support_session_required`, on an INSERT and on an UPDATE that would touch no row), and a support session writes that company and leaves **exactly one audit row per row**, naming the session's reason and the finding (`Ticket Fahrtenanalyse|same_street:r42|open`), with the platform account recorded as the reviewer.
  - **Measured, not assumed, on the VPS:** 131 migrations applied, 61 test files, **exit 0**, zero DIFF/ERROR/FAILED lines, `conflict-review-record: all 102 checks passed`, and `matrix: 405 lines, 0 differ from the recorded baseline, 8020 probes in 00:00:12.86`. The two `UNCOVERED` warnings name `public.uber_pull_note_skipped` and `public.uber_pull_note_unmatched` and are older than this branch. Locally: typecheck ratchet 176 errors at the baseline, style ratchet at the baseline, the targeted vitest suites passing (`conflictReviewRecord` 20, `conflictReviewTypes` 4, `backup` 22, `ReturnCheckPanel.render` 4) and `sqlComments` 349.

PR #304 (the repair pass) collided only in the four status documents, where both slices had added an entry at the top. After the resolution: no duplicate ordinals, exactly one `');'` in `_mx_spec` and one in `_mx_move`, both on the last row, the ten `_mx_expected` rows all ending in a comma with the list continuing, and the shared-shape list ending once. That the resolution is right is then a measurement rather than a reading - the matrix moved 400 lines/7920 probes to 405/8020, which is exactly PR #305's five lines, at `0 differ`. `backup.ts` and `backup.test.ts` carry the two tables in the **same** order, because that test compares the list order-sensitively.

A screen that calls `saveDetectedFindings` must ask `useCompanyScope().can('documents', 'edit')`, and `reviewFinding` must go through `updateChecked`.

  - **Both open questions are answered as of 24.10.2026, and neither moved a line of code.** The **month boundary** was the owner's: a finding whose evidence straddles one is reported **in both months**, each carrying its own decision - which is what already shipped, because `period_year` and `period_month` are in the idempotency index and the immutability trigger pins them. The **pre-finalisation checks** were left to me and stay a **hard gate with no override**; the reasoning is in the entry at the top of this file.
- **24.10.2026 - the Monatsplanung repair pass moved vehicle blocks in time to settle a driver's conflict, which is the owner's rule backwards (branch `feat/repair-pass-no-block-moves`, PR against `staging`, no migration, no SQL, nothing deployed).** The owner's rule is that **planning is daily and per vehicle, and drivers are assigned at month end** - a driver can pick up a fine, an accident or take leave mid-month, so his hours cannot be committed in advance. The vehicle's day is therefore the **fact** and the driver is **provisional**. `repairFinalOverlaps` did the opposite: a driver-side overlap was answered by relocating the vehicle's block in time, up to 200 iterations of it, rewriting `block_start_datetime`, `block_end_datetime`, `service_date`, `actual_start_ms` and `actual_end_ms`. It no longer does. A block whose assignment cannot hold loses its **driver**, keeps every one of its times, and is reported unassigned for a person to decide at month end. `src/utils/monthlyPlan/assign.ts` already refused to move blocks and recorded why; this module now keeps the same rule in the same vocabulary.
  - **Measured on production and on staging, read-only, and the measurement is the most important line in this entry: the pass was already doing nothing on real data.** Every planning run that exists on either stack is the same set - **11 runs, 4 applied and 7 replaced, one company (Y&A Mobility), months 05-08/2026**. The pass's own input was recovered from persisted data rather than re-derived: `fahrtenbuch_trips.assignment_block_id` is Phase 1's `vehicle_id|service_date|blockStart|blockEnd`, and the old move **never rewrote `block_id`**, so grouping the applied trips by it reproduces the block layout the pass received. **7295 trips tagged to a run, 0 with a missing or malformed block id, 0 cancelled, 0 without a driver, 0 blocks held by two drivers** - so the reconstruction covers the whole input. Over the **1290 reconstructed blocks** of the four applied runs: **conflictsBefore = 0 on every single run**, counting same-vehicle *and* same-driver overlapping pairs. So the old pass moved **0** blocks and the new one releases **0**. **The change is a no-op on every month that exists on either stack.**
  - **Two independent measurements agree, which is why this is not an artefact of the reconstruction.** (1) Same-vehicle **overlapping rides** across **all 8 imports** on production: **0** - so Phase 1 never had the input that makes it emit two overlapping blocks for one vehicle. (2) The persisted fingerprint of a historical move: `monthly_planning_manual_exceptions` stores `service_date`, `block_start_datetime` and `block_end_datetime` copied off the in-memory block, while its `block_id` still spells the pre-move times, so a row disagreeing with its own id is a move that actually happened. **12 of 12 rows agree, on both stacks** (`start_matches_utc` 12/12, `servicedate_matches` 12/12; the Berlin column reads 0/12 because the RPC casts a naive string under the session's zone - true of correct values too, and orthogonal to this). No block was ever moved before an exception was confirmed on it. Duplicate plates per company, the second structural path to a vehicle conflict: **0 of 18 cars**.

The owner held **252 + 266 of the 1290 applied blocks on production** (two `company_owner` records for Y&A Mobility) and **266 on staging** - roughly a fifth. The fuse was lit on a fifth of the blocks and still found nothing to act on.
  - **It was reachable in principle, though, and that is why this is not merely a tidy-up.** Phase 3 cannot produce a **driver** overlap: `checkOverlap` is applied at nine assignment sites, `validateClone` re-tests every simulated plan and `purgeFinalConflicts` sweeps last. But **nothing anywhere compares two blocks of one vehicle across two drivers** - `checkVehicleSwitch` skips the same vehicle and both it and `checkOneVehiclePerDay` are per driver - and Phase 1 emits overlapping blocks for one vehicle whenever the imported sheet holds a nested or overlapping ride, silently, with no coverage issue (its checks are `block_too_long`, `block_gap_too_large`, `duplicate_trip`, `missing_trip`). So one import with a nested ride would have fired the old relocation on a real month. The measurement says today's files have none; it does not say the next file will not.
  - **What an operator now sees.** The panel is renamed from *Konflikt-Reparatur* to *Konflikt-Prüfung*, and its two figures from *Konflikte vor/nach Reparatur* to *Konflikte erkannt* / *Konflikte offen* - three labels that still named a repair the pass no longer performs, inside the panel that now states *"Blockzeiten werden nie verschoben. Die Planung ist täglich und pro Fahrzeug; Fahrer werden am Monatsende zugewiesen."* The *Verschobene Blöcke* figure is replaced by *Ohne Fahrer gemeldet*, and each released block is listed with its sentence and also appears in the ordinary **Nicht zugewiesen** list carrying the same reason, where `applyManualAssignment` can take it - and that path applies the overlap check strictly, so the hard constraints still hold on a manual rescue.

So where the old pass would have quietly relocated a vehicle's day and let the month finalize, the month now **cannot** be finalized until a person assigns that block. That is the behaviour change to tell the owner about; on every month that exists it changes nothing, because zero blocks are released.

That machinery is Phase 3's `applyManualAssignment` / `applyDienstzeitException`, and **no Phase 3 file is in the diff at all**.

- **23.10.2026 (latest) - the month-end driver assignment becomes a record, and the gate that keeps it from being written too early (branch `feat/driver-month-assignment`, migration `20261023120000`, RLS kit run on the VPS: 178 of 178 in the new file, the matrix 385 lines with 0 differences, every other file green).** The owner's constraint of 22.10.2026: planning is daily and per vehicle, and assigning DRIVERS happens at month end, because a driver may pick up a fine, have an accident, meet something on the road or take leave in the course of it, so his hours cannot be committed in advance. `20261022140000` built the forward half with no driver column anywhere in it; this is the other half.
  - **What was inverted.** Everything downstream of the import treats ONE TRIP as the unit of assignment: `monatsplanungPhase4` emits one `ChangeRow` per trip, phase 5 updates trips one RPC call at a time, and `fahrtenbuch_trips` carries the assigned driver per row. A single mid-month accident therefore had to move dozens of rows, and **no column, step, flag or gate anywhere** said "these are this driver's hours" or "this driver was released from this month". The unit is now `public.driver_month_assignments`: one row per driver per month, which an incident moves in one call.
  - **What the record holds, and why each part is there.** The key `(company_id, year, month, driver_id)`; `plan_id`, the vehicle day plan it was made against (NOT NULL, because a release deletes the child rows and a record that cannot say what it stood for is not a record); a `draft` / `assigned` / `released` lifecycle; and **THE HOURS** as four integer columns the database computes itself - windows, wall-clock minutes, vehicles, operating days. The windows it stands for are rows in `driver_month_assignment_shifts`, for two reasons a number alone cannot serve: a month that says only "540 minutes" cannot be read back or compared with the vehicle plan, and **"a vehicle window has at most one driver" is a UNIQUE constraint** rather than a sentence in a comment. A release DELETES those rows, so that one constraint means "one LIVE claim per window" with no status column to drift, and the window is free for the next driver at once while the parent keeps the figures.
  - **The gate, and which clock it reads.** `app_private.driver_month_assignment_days_remaining(year, month)` is `greatest((first of the following month) - (today in Europe/Berlin), 0)`, and it is **the only place the rule is computed**. Europe/Berlin is a hard constant in some fifteen modules and `vitest.config.ts` pins `TZ=Europe/Berlin`; no per-company timezone was introduced. The helper is STABLE and not IMMUTABLE, which is also why the gate cannot be a CHECK.
  - **What the gate does when opened early: it is allowed and never silent.** A row written while days remain must carry `early_reason` or it is refused with the hint `driver_month_assignment_month_not_ended`; when it carries one, **the database** sets `opened_early` and stamps `early_days_remaining` with the number IT measured, so the record says how early it was and not how early the caller claimed. All three columns are then part of the row's fixed key, so the warning cannot be erased. The pairing is a CHECK (`opened_early = (early_reason IS NOT NULL) AND opened_early = (early_days_remaining IS NOT NULL)`), which is the half a CHECK can carry. **The gate is in the GUARD, not only in the RPC**, so a second caller writing the table directly meets the same question; the RPC asks the same helper beforehand only so it can refuse by return value with the number of days, which is what lets a screen offer "open it anyway, and say why". The gate is on OPENING alone - committing and releasing are never gated by the clock, because the incident happens inside the month.
  - **The three RPCs**, all `documents`-gated, all VOLATILE, all refusing by return value and raising only on a broken contract: `driver_month_assignment_save(jsonb)` (closed payload keys, and `plan_id` is **not** one - the month's confirmed plan is looked up, so an assignment cannot be built on a proposal), `_commit(uuid)` (re-derives under the month's advisory lock that the plan is still active and that **a driver is not in two places at once**, in one pass and never a self-join, and writes the four figures from the windows themselves) and `_release(uuid, text, text)` (deletes the windows under a withdrawal marker, records the reason, keeps the figures). **The closed list of release reasons - the owner's own four plus `other` - lives in the CHECK constraint and nowhere else**, so the RPC cannot drift from it; an unknown code is reported as that constraint's name.
  - **What was deliberately NOT touched, and why it is the point.** Phase 1, phase 3, phase 4, the repair pass, the finalization checks, `computeLohnartSeconds` and every document builder: unchanged, unread, unreferenced. That code encodes statutory German payroll rules more intricate than its shape suggests, has almost no test coverage and produces documents that go to a Steuerberater, so rewiring it onto this record is a later slice needing a before/after comparison on a real month on staging. (6) A CI job, `osrm` in `pr-checks.yml`, that runs the chain for real when a diff touches it.
  - **Where it runs, and why (the brief left it open).** An **edge function, not a Kong route.** The container has no authentication of its own and sits on a host shared with another live product; a Kong route would be open to anyone holding the anon key, which ships in the bundle, and the only rate limit Kong could add is a new plugin (`KONG_PLUGINS` is a rollback guard). The function asks GoTrue for a *person* and the database for an *active company* (`get_active_company_id()`, the helper every business table asks), validates and caps the request (1-100 coordinate pairs, strict types), calls one constant address and logs counts. Not a route on an existing function: none fits, and an outbound call on `send-document` or `manage-users` would widen workers that hold SMTP or the service key. Its `FUNCTION_ENV` entry is the base variables only. The container's address is a constant in `travel-route-core.ts` (`http://osrm:5000`), not a variable, so the compose file's `functions` block did not change: a value that can be typed wrong can be aimed at the database, and `tests/deploy/osrm.test.ts` ties host and port to the compose service. Kong, `kong.yml`, `ci-release.sh` and the host action are untouched, so **no wrapper reinstall is needed**.
  - **Rules that are easy to undo.** (a) **It takes coordinates, never addresses**: a passenger's address reaches neither the function nor the container, and nothing logs a coordinate (the container runs at WARNING; measured in CI: at the default level the same container logs every request's path, coordinates included, and the client's address, and at WARNING its log is empty; CI fails if the log ever holds a coordinate the live test asked about, and runs that control every time). (b) **A lookup that fails is not "no".** Every failure is a reason on the pair it happened to (`no_route`, `not_on_road`, `service_error`, `bad_answer`, `unreachable`, `timeout`, `too_far_from_road`, `address_not_located`, ...); nothing answers a duration it did not read from an `Ok`. There is **no fallback to the old haversine x 1.3** and there must not be one: it would turn *nicht prüfbar* into *bestanden*. (c) **OSRM has no traffic**, so `departureMs` is not sent, the minutes are a floor, `confidence` is `medium` at best (`low` when the locator was unsure of an address) and the company's `travel_margin_minutes` is where its buffer for traffic lives. That setting still has **no product default**; the hook does nothing while it is unset, as the analysis does. (d) `MAX_SNAP_METERS = 250` (`estimate.ts`): OSRM snaps any point to the nearest road however far, so a located address more than 250 m from a road is unavailable. A plausibility bound, **tuned on no real data**, written in one place and pinned at its boundary. (e) `returnCheck/geo.ts` is untouched: "Luftlinie" stays a straight line, and a road distance from here is a second, labelled figure. (f) The data format belongs to the OSRM version that wrote it: moving the pin in the compose file means running the build script again, and the guard enforces it through `ready.json`'s `image`.
  - **What a release has to do on the host.** *Merging is inert:* the next staging release replaces the compose file and `deploy.sh`, adds the function, recreates `functions` (as every release does), starts nothing new and pulls nothing; `COMPOSE_PROFILES=staging` still passes the new check, and so does production's empty value. *Turning it on is the owner's, per stack, staging first:* (1) put `deploy/osrm-build-data.sh` next to `deploy.sh` on the host (mode 755; the wrapper does not ship it); (2) `./osrm-build-data.sh --check` prints the plan and whether this host can (exit 3 if not); (3) run it detached - it refuses unless memory and disk fit, runs each step in a container without a network and with a memory ceiling below what the host has free, proves the new build loads as the service's user, and restarts nothing - and prefer `--region europe/germany/nordrhein-westfalen` first, to prove the pipeline on 915 MB before Germany's 4.5 GiB; (4) add `osrm` to `COMPOSE_PROFILES` in that stack's `.env` (staging: `staging,osrm`); (5) release: the guard checks the build, then `osrm` starts; (6) `docker compose --profile osrm ps` must say healthy, then call `/functions/v1/travel-route` once with a real staging user's token (`{"pairs":[{"id":"x","from":{"lat":51.1657,"lon":7.0671},"to":{"lat":51.2277,"lon":6.7735}}]}`); (7) production the same way, with its own build or the volume copied. *Turning it off:* remove `osrm` from `COMPOSE_PROFILES` **and** `docker compose --profile osrm rm -sf osrm` - compose does not stop a container whose profile is no longer named (expected, not tried). A refresh is the same script, then `docker compose --profile osrm up -d --force-recreate --no-deps osrm`. `OSRM_MEM_LIMIT` (default 12G) is a starting point to move after `docker stats`.

One later run failed before building anything on a 60-second timeout reading Geofabrik's snapshot page (`curl: (28)`); the extract's own download already retried and the three small requests did not, so they retry now, pinned by a test. **The container answers:** 30 routes in about 120 to 150 ms through `routePairs`, all `Ok`, and it names its map (`data_version` 2026-10-20T20:23:47Z, which is the source label `osrm@2026-10`); the running container is `user=10001:10001 readonly=true caps_dropped=[ALL] memory=12884901888 pids=64 ports=map[]`; a point in Munich asked of the Düsseldorf map came back as a route of 23 km with the point **455 km** from the road it was put on, which the estimate policy turns into `too_far_from_road` (a fleet outside the built region gets "nicht prüfbar", never a made-up drive). **The function answers too, in the stack's own edge runtime:** the job starts `supabase/edge-runtime:v1.76.2` (the version `deploy/docker-compose.yml` runs) with the repository's real `main` router and `travel-route`, the real container behind it and a small stub standing in for GoTrue's `GET /auth/v1/user` and the `get_active_company_id()` RPC (`tests/deploy/edge-stub.mjs`, keyed by the token's `sub`), and `tests/deploy/edge-e2e.mjs` asks over HTTP: no token is a 401 from the router; the anon key, which the router admits because this stack signed it, is a 401 `not_authenticated` from the function; a person without an active company is a 403 `no_company`; two pairs are a 200 with the map's `data_version` and the results in request order; the pair far outside the map comes back as a route with its 455 km snap distance rather than as a failure (the estimator then refuses it); 101 pairs are a 413, a latitude of 91, a repeated id and text that is not JSON are each a 400, a GET is a 405, the preflight from the app origin is allowed and from another origin is not; and **with the container stopped** the answer is still a 200 with `unreachable` on every pair, no number and no `data_version`. The function also type-checks under Deno 2.1.4 (`deno check`, in an isolated copy of `supabase/functions`: next to the repository's `package.json` Deno looks for `node_modules` and refuses the edge-runtime types' own npm imports, which says nothing about the function). **Build cost, six builds** (the CI runs of this branch whose logs were kept; the job builds the map again on every push that touches these files): extract 125 to 159 s, partition 10 to 12 s, customize 3 to 4 s, 323 MB on disk; the tools' own peak memory (five of the six; the first only sampled it) 1.05 to 1.09 GiB, 0.26 GiB and 0.22 GiB. OSRM's wiki table scaled to this extract (415 / 220 / 174 GiB and 300 GB for the 61 GiB planet of 11/2021 on v5.26, "sizes scale roughly linear") says 1.4 GiB and 1.0 GB, so it errs high by a quarter for memory and threefold for disk. Scaled by size to Germany's 4.5 GiB the measured runs give about 24 GiB at the extract's peak, 7 GB of data and an hour on two CPUs (wiki-scaled: 31 GiB, 22 GB, 9 GiB to serve). **Extrapolations across a factor of 22, not measurements: the script refuses on the wiki's larger figures, and the first real build writes the true ones into `ready.json`.**
  - **How far the old estimate was, on 300 invented pairs (60 per band, 0.5 to 20 km of straight line, drawn around Solingen with a seeded generator, so the table is the same every run; real pairs are passengers' places and were not used).** Road distance was a median **1.60 times** the straight line (p10 to p90 1.26 to 2.69), against the 1.3 of `simulatedRides/geo.ts`; as time, OSRM took a median 0.98 of the old model's minutes overall and 0.64 to 1.93 at p10 to p90. By band (OSRM minutes / old-model minutes at 14:00, median): 0.5-1 km **1.54**, 1-2 km 1.28, 2-5 km 1.03, 5-10 km 0.80, 10-20 km **0.73**. The old model is right on average and wrong in opposite directions at the two ends: a short hop takes about half as long again as it said, a long drive a quarter less. OSRM's minutes are free-flow and ignore the rush hour (the old model's 21 km/h), so the margin setting still has work to do. Table in the PR.

RPCs `vehicle_day_plan_save(jsonb)` and `vehicle_day_plan_confirm(uuid, boolean)`, two trigger functions and two helpers in `app_private`. Client `src/utils/vehicleDayPlanPersistence.ts` (save, confirm, save-and-confirm, load by id or by month), outside the pure engine; `boundary.test.ts` passes unchanged. `BACKUP_TABLES` carries both tables.

The codebase has four cuts of "operating day" (04:00 configurable in the recommender, 04:00 hard-coded in `simulatedRides/time.ts`, 04:00 for Uber in `uberPeriods.ts`, 00:00 calendar in Phase 1/3 and `monthlyPlan/blocks.ts`); a plan that does not say which cut built it cannot be read back. (2) No driver column anywhere, **and no free-form place for one**: the kit pins the exact column list, self-check 9 scans the catalogue, the save RPC refuses any payload key it does not know, `summary` is a closed object of fourteen numeric keys (`app_private.vehicle_day_plan_summary_problem`, the one definition, applied by the plan guard to every insert and every edit of a draft and by the RPC before it writes), every field of a shift must arrive as the JSON type it is stored as, and `algorithm_version` is a token by a CHECK. `vehicle` is the one free-text field and stays one: the database cannot tell a plate from another short string.   - **The review, and what it changed.** An adversarial reviewer ran the migration against a replica and reproduced everything below before anything was changed. **F1: `vehicle_day_plan_confirm` compared every shift with every other.** Right after a bulk save the planner's figures do not know the new plan, it expects one row, takes a nested loop with the plan as the only index condition, and compares all pairs: 3100 shifts took 2 to 3.5 s on a quiet machine and 5 to 11 s on a busy one, 12,400 shifts never finished inside the API roles' 8 s statement timeout (cancelled in 5 of 5 runs here), and the header had claimed 0.1 s from an empty table. It is now one pass in start order (a running maximum of the ends per vehicle): 3100 shifts confirm in 0.01 s, 12,400 in 0.02 s, right after the save. The old query is kept in the kit as the oracle. **F2: a race.** The shift guard read its plan's status with no lock, so a shift INSERTED while a confirmation was open landed in the confirmed plan afterwards (a confirmed plan with two overlapping shifts), and a shift DELETE did not even wait (a confirmed plan with no shift, the thing `plan_empty` exists to prevent). `parent_is_open` reads the plan `FOR KEY SHARE` now, which conflicts with the `FOR UPDATE` the confirmation takes; the new kit file `tests/rls/vehicle-day-two-sessions.sql` runs four scenarios with two dblink sessions. **F3: rule 2 had doors.** `summary` was accepted verbatim (a driver id, a list of rides), `jsonb_to_recordset` turned any JSON value into the text of a vehicle (an object became a "vehicle"), and `algorithm_version` was any 100 characters: all closed (above); the client sends the months as YYYYMM numbers and leaves an absent target out, because a null is not a number. **F4: the migration's self-check proved that names exist, not that conditions hold** (a trigger wired to the wrong function, or `IF false AND <the condition>`, passed it): it now reads the bodies through `app_private.function_code` (comments removed), matches each load-bearing condition whole, requires each table to carry its own guard, and runs the summary helper on literals. **F5 to F8: the documentation said things the tables do not enforce** (`generation` is not a count, `shift_index` is not required to follow start order, the vehicle is its exact text, the check is per plan, "three trigger functions" was two plus a helper); each is now stated as it is, and both RPCs pin `pg_catalog` first in their `search_path`. Not changed, as the reviewer said no action was needed: a plan-id existence oracle inherited from the monthly plan, and no upper bound on the shifts of a payload (the 8 s timeout is the bound; 12,400 shifts, 100 vehicles x 31 days x 4, save in 1.2 to 2.4 s here).

A missing GRANT is now reported by what was refused, read out of the message (`privilege table vehicle_day_plans`), a HINT counts as a reason only when it is a snake_case word, and the file runs its probe against a refusal written with and without that hint. The two tables stay two different lines, a policy refusal still prints its own message and an RPC's gate its hint: nothing was folded into one matcher.

What it lacked is what a reader needs to weigh a row, and the Blitzer is the case that decided the design: the fine arrives weeks after the event, and a `must_include_in_plan` note is read as evidence the driver was at the wheel at that moment. No events engine was built.
  - **What was added.** Thirteen columns: `occurred_at`, `reported_at` (both set by a person, both NULL for "not recorded"), `received_at` (stamped by a BEFORE trigger, never the client's), `entry_source` (`manual` / `driver_app` / `system` / `legacy`, stamped), `evidence_path`, `verification_status` (`unverified` / `verified` / `rejected`) with `reviewed_by` / `reviewed_at` stamped from the session and a mandatory `rejected_reason`, `latitude` / `longitude` / `location_accuracy_m`, and `change_log`. Twelve CHECKs, each with a name of its own so a refusal says which rule spoke, none calling a function outside `pg_catalog`. The trigger `driver_notes_provenance_guard` (SECURITY DEFINER, `app_private`) stamps, pins and logs. No policy was touched or restated, none reads a new column (asserted), and `driver_notes` keeps its four policies and both context triggers.

Every existing row is labelled `entry_source = 'legacy'` by the column default at ADD COLUMN, which writes no row. **The migration contains no UPDATE of `driver_notes`**: no `updated_at` moves, and a backfill by UPDATE would also have failed on any database where `driver_notes_behavior_follows_type` stayed NOT VALID, because PostgreSQL checks that constraint on every UPDATE of a row that breaks it (measured in `note-type-constraint.sql`). `received_at` is NULL on legacy rows too (`created_at` is their only stamp); `legacy` is a word and not a NULL so "not recorded" cannot be mistaken for "forgot to stamp".
  - **The evidence path is a CHECK, not a function, and stricter than `receipts_document_prefix`.** `<company_id>/driver-notes/<note_id>/<uuid>.<pdf|jpg|jpeg|png|webp>` in the private `documents` bucket: the company folder (what the storage policies key on), the note's own id, a generated name (an uploaded "Bussgeld_Mueller.pdf" would carry a name), no SVG or HTML (a document served inline from the API origin executes its script, 20260928100000). `receipts_document_prefix` admits `<company>/../<other>/x` and any extension, and a NULL company with a path; this one refuses all three. A bucket key, never a URL. One file per note; several would be a child table. No storage policy was added or restated.

For a caller with a session the trigger now writes `created_by` from `auth.uid()` on INSERT, pins it on UPDATE and forces `submitted_by_name` to NULL; a writer with no session (service role, migration, psql) may still repair them. No screen shows `created_by`; the Notizen Excel prints it as an id.
  - **Change history lives in the row** (`change_log`, the shape of `driver_month_budget.recompute_log`): one entry per UPDATE that changed a tracked field, `{at, by, changed, previous}`. Structured fields keep their old value; **free text is named and never kept** (`note_text` is the column the support-write audit already will not copy, and a log that preserved every earlier wording would keep a diagnosis somebody typed and then corrected). `note_date` is not tracked: the screen recomputes it to the minute on every save, and counting it took a verification back on a save that changed nothing (probes 140 and 141, mutation M9). The cost, stated: deleting a note deletes its history, and so does deleting its author's account (`created_by` cascades from `auth.users`, which predates this).

Nothing is resolved quietly.

A `Phase3Result` does not carry the map its plan was made with (`options` keeps three settings), and putting one in the result would freeze the notes at plan time while the screen re-reads them; required, so a caller that forgets it fails the typecheck ratchet (still 179). The preview passes the map it already loads (no second query) to both calls, **and lists it in the dependencies of the `resolverCandidates` memo**: those were hand-listed under an eslint-disable next to a comment saying `selectedDrivers` was enough, and the notes load asynchronously. **Tests:** `monatsplanungPhase3.manualNotes.test.ts` (39 cases: a whole day, a time inside a day, a time across midnight, a range, every boundary including the two exact-midnight ones, both DST days with a guard that the zone is Berlin, which notes count, `applyManualAssignment`; - **21.10.2026 (latest) - the gap between two rides of one vehicle (branch `fix/simulated-approach-leg`, PR against `staging`, no migration).** Measured on the generated September file against the real `uber.xlsx`: implied speed from one ride's order position to the next (distance between the two `Standort` values over next start minus previous end; a Zielort has no coordinates in a file) had median 95 km/h and 38.5 % of transitions over 120 km/h (49 % on the owner's file) against the real 17.7 and 5.8 %. Rides inside were fine. **Rule, header of `generator.ts`:** gap >= travel(previous Zielort -> new Standort -> new Abholort), two legs; an order that reached the car during the previous ride (34 % in the real file, 34 % generated) has its Standort on that ride's route and only Zielort -> Abholort remains. `driveSeconds` (no 45 s pickup handling) is the first leg, `deadheadSeconds` the second; `validateRides` checks both legs and that the order cannot arrive before the first leg is driven. The gap also carries a wait for the order (log-normal, median 9 min, capped 100) so the real median gap (12.6 min) is met; the wait is shortened, never the legs, at the end of a shift, with a 41 s margin so a shift stays >= 4 h. **Decision, do not undo: the approach is a time constraint and never a row** - a row would put a journey without a passenger into the Fahrtenbuch (18 passenger columns) and a no-fare row would enter the counts and break the cent-exact match of the fares to umsatz/bargeld/trinkgeld. **Not zero on purpose:** the real file has 5.8 % over 120 km/h (max 31021 km/h); the waits aim at about that, `approachLeg.test.ts` asserts 3 % to 10 %. Ride length is log-normal (median 6.1, sigma 0.873, cap 95 km, matching the real quartiles) and a length the pool or the remaining shift cannot hold is redrawn, not piled on an edge. Measured after (6 seeds): city-sized pool 5.3 % over 120, median 20 km/h, p95 123; 90 km pool 4.0 %, median 16.4, p95 106, ride length q25/q50/q75/q95/max 4.0/6.2/10.9/24.7/95 (city pool: median 5.4, pool-limited). The old test "at most 40 s longer than the drive" is gone (the gap now includes the wait); `generator.test.ts` keeps the lower bound. Negative controls run: no approach term and no wait fails 4 tests (64.6 % over 120); one leg instead of two fails the validator and the leg test (the speed test still passes, because the wait compensates). **Not verified:** a live Nominatim pool; a generated file opened by eye.
- **21.10.2026 (latest) - deleting an invoice (branch `fix/invoice-delete`, PR against `staging`, migration `20261021120000`, RLS kit not run).** **Step-1 measurement, from the code:** the delete button was **missing**, not silently broken. `SubscriptionBillingPage`'s row menu offers View, Mark paid (cash), Mark unpaid (paid rows), Cancel, PDF. `CompanyBillingPage` shows invoices read-only and has no delete (left absent: the policies have no company write term and giving one would let a customer erase its own billing history and withdraw its own access). `InvoiceDetailModal`, `MarkPaidModal` and `GenerateInvoicesModal` have none. No `.delete()` on `subscription_invoices` exists in `src/`; the only direct write on the table is `GenerateInvoicesModal`'s INSERT, and an INSERT refused by RLS raises an error rather than reporting success, so it needs no affected-count check. **Why not a direct DELETE:** since D14 the SELECT policy is the tenant term alone; a DELETE naming a column also passes the SELECT policy, so for a platform account outside a support session it removes 0 rows and PostgREST answers 200 (`matrix.sql` records the D cell as `..`). **What was built:** `public.platform_invoice_delete(p_invoice_id)`, a sibling of `platform_invoice_cancel` (`billing.manage` first via `platform_rpc_authorize`, one audit row `invoice.delete` whose before values are number, amount, period and the withdrawn coverage end). `status = 'paid'` answers `{success:false, reason:'invoice_paid'}`; an invoice with any `new_status = 'paid'` row in `subscription_payment_audit` answers `invoice_was_paid` (that table cascades from the invoice, so deleting would erase the payment trail). Both audit as an `error` row and answer a German sentence built in the function (the shared `platform_rpc_response` is not restated; its ELSE would print the generic sentence). Otherwise: coverage row `status='void', void_reason='invoice_deleted'`, DELETE, `recompute_company_subscription`. **FK checked:** `subscription_coverage.source_id` is a plain uuid with no foreign key, so deleting the invoice alone would orphan a live period and keep the company admitted; hence the explicit void. `invoice_deleted` is deliberately not `invoice_canceled`, the reason `subscription_invoice_apply` and `mark_paid` revive. **Screen:** a Loeschen/Delete item in the row menu for every non-paid invoice (hidden for a paid one; the database refuses regardless), a confirm dialog, and the refusal mapped by reason code to `sa.subs.deleteRefused.*` so it follows the UI language; no new inline styles (token classes). **Known:** `generate_invoice_number` is max+1 over the remaining rows, so deleting a year's newest invoice frees its number; only never-paid invoices can go. A cancelled, never-paid invoice can be deleted and keeps `invoice_canceled` on its period. **Kit needed:** `npm run test:rls` on the VPS - `subscriptions.sql` section 11 (11a deleted, voided, company refused, one audit row; 11b not_found; 11c invoice_paid with invoice, coverage and admission untouched; 11d invoice_was_paid, a different reason; 11e cancelled then deleted; 11f grants and shape; 11g builds two mutants from `pg_get_functiondef` and requires the probes' observables to move), `platform-rpcs.sql` (EXECUTE list and role row `YNYNN`), `matrix.sql` (rpc line `PNNNNNY`). None of that SQL has been parsed by PostgreSQL yet.

Callers derive it from their trips or import: Preview (trips), Finalize and Historical Reconciliation (`importsAreSimulated`, which throws on a failed lookup so an unknown source never prints as real), MonthlyPlanPage (trips), Historical Working Hours (`writeMarkedWorkbook`, four Fahrtenbuch writers). Monthly-plan documents go through `markSimulated()` (preview footnote, file name) plus each builder content marker (PDF stamp, payroll notice line, planned-Fahrtenbuch notice sheet). **Saved Stundennachweise:** `saved_stundennachweise.is_simulated` (same migration) is derived by trigger from `source_run_id` and sticky (a caller may mark more, never less), because `source_import_id` was never written and the stored PDF in `stundennachweise-pdfs` is built before DocumentsPage ever sees the record. The shift recommendation drops simulated rides before learning. `generateMonth` (invented fares) is deleted. The readers inventory has only marks / counts. **Not done:** Belege and notes reconciliation (slice two, adds consistency not safety, not needed to merge); screen banners exist on the trips list, the Preview and the trip analysis only; DocumentsPage list shows no badge; nothing was rendered in a browser or opened as a real PDF by eye (the PDF stamp is asserted on the PDF bytes, the XLSX notice by reading the workbook back).
- **20.10.2026 (later) - the generator now explains recorded income, and the wall is per driver-week.** Owner: the generated logbook must depend on the figures the system holds. `generateFromFigures` (`figures.ts`) reads `income` per driver and business week (Monday-Sunday) and makes rides whose fares sum, in integer cents, to `umsatz`; cash-paid fares to `bargeld`; tips to `trinkgeld`; the last ride of a group absorbs the remainder. `aktionen` is carried by no ride and left as recorded. No income row means no rides; a contradiction (cash over or without revenue, tips without revenue, negative or sub-cent amount, unknown driver, revenue under one fare, figures the shift rules cannot explain) is listed as a finding and that driver-week is refused. The card offers 15, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180 minutes and 6, 12, 14, 18, 24 hours (stored values outside the list are still added). The hint no longer interpolates a number.

It skips any send or reminder moment at or before `armed_at` using the same whole-Berlin-wall-minute comparison, so the answer is the week after; the reminder is null unless reminder and driver mail are both on; a reminder whose lead crosses midnight carries its own day and weekday. A reminder still inside its 30-minute window counts as next (it will go out). - **19.10.2026 - the operational Excel columns match Uber's: no number format, no unit, no currency symbol, no widths (branch `feat/export-uber-columns`, PR against `staging`, no migration, RLS kit not run).** The owner opened a real Belege file beside `uber.xlsx` and the columns still differed. Measured in uber.xlsx's XML: `styles.xml` has zero `<numFmt>` entries and `cellXfs count="2"` (default, and the header's bold + border + alignment); header cells `s="1"`, data cells no `s` at all; no `<cols>`, `<autoFilter>`, `<pane>`, `<mergeCell>`. So the payload carries no `fmt` for any operational column and the service writes data cells with no style index. `width` and `align` never reached the file in the plain path (the payload has no field for them), so there is no `<cols>`; that is now pinned.

  - **Percent is the exception: its VALUE changed, not only its look.** A bare fraction would read as a different quantity (0.42 is not "a plainer 42 %"), so `buildPlainSheet` writes a `percent` column as stored value times 100, bare: `0.42` becomes `42`, `0.4147` becomes `41.47`, no `%`, no format (`fractionToPercent`, rounded to twelve significant digits to drop float noise such as 0.29*100 = 28.999999999999996). Anyone comparing an old export with a new one: the three percent columns now hold 42 where they held 0.42. Verified before scaling: Umsätze `Anteil` is `share(sum, total)` = part/whole, Gehälter `Anteil` is `salary.salary_ratio`, Fahrer `Gehaltsanteil` is `d.salary_ratio` (numeric(5,4), CHECK 0..1, the driver form divides by 100); all three are fractions, so none is scaled twice. - **19.10.2026 - Abrechnung: confirm that a driver handed the cash back (branch `feat/abrechnung-cash-handover`, PR against `staging`, not merged, migration `20261019110000`).** Owner: each weekly row gets an action that opens a popup with one amount, defaulting to the row's Difference (`bar_zuruck`) and editable, then shows the cash given and a status. Two owner decisions held as given: **a record only** (the Bargeldbestand must not move; `cashLedger.ts` already counts a driver's cash as in the till from the day its `income.type = 'bargeld'` row is dated, so booking a movement would count it twice) and **the amount is editable** (partial hand-over is normal).
  - **Store the amount, derive the status.** `public.abrechnung_handovers (company_id, year, month, week_number, driver_name, driver_id, amount numeric(12,2) >= 0, confirmed_by, updated_by, ...)`, UNIQUE on `(company_id, year, month, week_number, driver_name)`, which is the identity the Abrechnung itself uses. The status is computed in `src/utils/abrechnungHandover.ts` in integer cents: `given` (handed over >= due; the excess is shown), `partial` (the rest is shown), `open` (nothing handed over), and `none_due` (the Difference is zero or negative). That is three states plus one: the owner named two, his own 30-of-50 example makes the third. **0 is an answer**: confirming 0 writes a row of 0.00 (shown `0,00 EUR`, status open); no row shows a dash. Both derive `open`.
  - **Monthly view** sums the driver's weekly records and derives against the monthly Difference. Confirming is weekly only (a note on the screen says so); the monthly row has no week to key on.
  - **No RPC.** The screen upserts on the key. A SECURITY INVOKER BEFORE trigger (`app_private.abrechnung_handovers_guard`, which names only `public`, `pg_catalog` and `auth.uid()`) stamps `confirmed_by`/`updated_by`/timestamps and resolves `driver_id` when the name matches exactly one ACTIVE driver of the company (case and repeated spaces ignored, as `abrechnung_reminder_facts` does); two matches, none or an inactive driver give NULL. `driver_id` is not part of the key, so an ambiguous or unmatched name is still recordable. It is a FK with ON DELETE SET NULL.
  - **Shape.** Four policies; SELECT is the tenant term or the read seam; every write repeats one predicate as USING and WITH CHECK plus `current_role_permits('income', true)`. The page is `income` (the Abrechnung is built on it); `cash-balance` would imply a till write. No `page_key` was created, so `PAGE_DEFINITIONS` and `role_page_keys()` are untouched. Both context triggers (`refuse_read_only_context_write`, `record_support_write`) are on. anon holds nothing, the service role only SELECT. The migration ends with a self-check that fails the release if any of that, or the guard's SECURITY INVOKER-ness, its absence of `app_private.` references, or its absence of any ledger table name, is lost.
  - **Audit decision:** a support session's write is recorded with the amount and the driver name in clear (`amount` does not match `support_write_redaction_pattern()` for this table; it is a hand-over, not pay).
  - **Limitation, not invented here:** the Abrechnung identifies a driver by free-text name, so **renaming a driver orphans the record** (it stays under the old name). A real fix needs a driver id on `income` and `receipts`.
  - **A figure whose load failed is not shown.** The hand-over records load with the rows; a failure of either fails the load, so the screen shows its existing failure alert and never "still with driver" for everybody. A failed re-read after a save does the same.
  - **Gates measured.** `npm run build` (typecheck ratchet 179 = baseline, style ratchet at baseline, full vitest, vite build): **exit 0 on the final run**; the first full run failed three tests that are timeouts under load (they were running beside a browser flow) (`WerkstattPage.week.test.ts` and two in `tests/deploy/google-signin-guards.test.ts`, each green when run alone). **RLS kit on the VPS, run to completion, exit 0** (the real ssh exit code): the new `tests/rls/abrechnung-handovers.sql` passes, and `matrix.sql` reports 365 lines, 0 differ, 7220 probes, with five new lines for the table (`PP Y. ...` for S, `PP RR YR YR YR RY RR` for I, and so on, cash_transactions' cells with anon holding nothing) and the move entry. **Mutation controls on the kit file, each run through the whole kit with the migration's own self-check stripped so the kit file had to catch it:** UPDATE without the gate, UPDATE without WITH CHECK, either context trigger dropped, the guard not stamping `confirmed_by`, the guard not restricting the driver lookup to the company, the guard accepting inactive drivers, the wrong page, an anon grant, a negative amount allowed. A first draft of the company-restriction probe was **vacuous** (as the editor, RLS hides company B's driver anyway, so removing the guard's own company term changed nothing); it now inserts as the table owner and the mutation is caught. The matrix itself (the S/I/U/D/M cells) agreed with the recorded lines on the clean run; it was not separately mutation-tested because the kit aborts at the first failing file and the shape section of the new file fails first.

The batch-2 harness flow has **13 failures on this branch and 13 on the unmodified base** (stale fixtures in Gehälter and Bargeldbestand); none are in the Abrechnung checks, which pass.

All three were needed to keep 375 px without sideways scroll once a second 40 px action existed.

  - **The compose block was invalid and it refused two staging releases, measured on the host.** The service was written with a top-level `pids_limit: 128` beside `deploy.resources.limits: { memory: 512M }`. Compose normalises `pids_limit` into `deploy.resources.limits.pids`, and when the limits map is present in the file it reads the absent key as 0, then refuses the whole project with `can't set distinct values on 'pids_limit' and 'deploy.resources.limits.pids'` because 128 is not 0. `deploy.sh`'s first guard is `docker compose config`, so **the releases of #251 (`69b7783`) and #252 (`1703ef6`) both failed there and changed nothing** — `releases/current` stayed at `20261019T085318Z-9c1da5e`, which is why `/export/v1/` answered 404 on staging and the old writer was still producing the files. The cap is `pids: 128` inside the limits map now, and nothing else in this stack sets a process cap, so this was the only place it could bite. Measured on the host (Docker Compose v5.5.0) against all four spellings: `pids_limit` beside an explicit limits map is refused; `pids` inside the map, both spellings at the same value, and `pids_limit` with no `deploy` block are each accepted. The real file now renders `pids: 128` with `config -q` exiting 0. **It was never caught locally because there is no Docker here and no gate parses this file** — the same class as *CI is green on SQL it never parses*.
  - **Shape (added the same day, owner: "literally the same as Uber's file").** `exportTableToExcel`/`exportSheetsToExcel` now build `buildPlainWorkbook`: headers in A1, data from A2, no title/module/timestamp/filter line/totals row/footer/empty-state text, no autofilter, no widths. **Information removed on purpose:** which filter produced the file, and the "Gesamt" sum. Numbers stay numbers under their formats (3-decimal unit price included), a missing figure stays an empty cell (never 0), header text stays in the UI language. Sheet key `header: true` styles row 1 like Uber's (decoded from its styles.xml: bold, thin border on four sides, horizontal centre, vertical top). Stripped in the new plain builder, not in `buildTableWorkbook`, which `monthlyPlanDocumentBuilders.ts` (not on the service) still uses and whose cell-by-cell tests are unchanged. The Fahrtenanalyse report keeps its multi-block layout.

  - **Moved onto the service:** `exportTableToExcel`, `exportSheetsToExcel` (so every panel, Belege, Umsätze, Gehälter and archive export) and the Fahrtenanalyse report. **Still on SheetJS/ExcelJS (follow-up, needs committed goldens first):** `fahrtenbuchExport.ts`, `fahreruebersichtExport.ts`, `monatsplanungXlsxExport.ts`, `monthlyPlanFahrtenbuchExport.ts`, `monthlyPlanDocumentBuilders.ts`, `HistoricalWorkingHoursWizard.tsx`, `MonatsplanungAssignmentPreview.tsx`, `MonatsplanungStundennachweisPreview.tsx`. `styledWorkbookDownload.ts` stays for the Fahrerübersicht and the monthly plan documents.
  - **The brief's premise that was only half right, measured.** The sample `uber.xlsx` was re-saved by Excel: `lastModifiedBy` is a person, `app.xml` says Microsoft Excel 16.03, the workbook carries Excel's `absPath` of the owner's own folder, and strings are shared strings. openpyxl itself writes `inlineStr`, no `sharedStrings.xml`, `docProps/app.xml` first and `[Content_Types].xml` last, and `Application` = `Microsoft Excel Compatible / Openpyxl 3.1.5`. The sample's header row is also bold, bordered and centred (a pandas-style header); this phase follows the brief's decision (plain) and does not reproduce it.

The first export of a user after a service restart pays a GoTrue round trip.

After: the same formula over the rows that now exist, floored at zero as a whole; for a period with no negative row the result is byte-identical. `salaryDue.ts` rule 5. A negative cash figure is still carried as `SkippedFigure` / `uber_pull_runs.skipped` (the reporting from #244 is kept, for cash only; the Alert text now says cash).

The floor is on the TOTAL, so a reversed tip and a positive revenue share net against each other. Floats stay (converting the salary path to integer cents is a separate change); the arithmetic is the old expression and only the floor and the rounded remainder are new. `sumIncomeAmount` is the old inline reduce moved out so a test can pin that every row counts. `SalariesManagement` shows a caution Alert (driver, amount, period) and a marker in the total column; the Gehälter Excel has a "Nicht verrechnet" column and a summary row; the driver's salary PDF states it. **Carrying the remainder into the next period is deliberately not built** - a larger design with its own questions (which period, what if the driver leaves); the number is on screen so a person can act.
